title: Building a design team for four Shopify apps
title_html: Building a design team for four Shopify apps
hook: From a ticket queue stretched across four apps to a team that ships one merchant experience.
dek: In twelve months I grew design from a ticket queue into a team with pods, rituals, a budget and a monthly page leadership reads.
team: Product designers and a research & content designer, partnering with the PMs and engineering leads
register_line: Handoff −35% · budget within 3% · no one has left
tldr: The ask: one design team for four apps, with numbers leadership could read.
I reorganized design into three pods and a research seat, hired on one written rubric and started crit.
Every month I gather a HEART scorecard per app and send leadership one page.
A year on: no one has left, handoff −35%, budget within 3%.

challenge.inherited: “I file the ticket and hope design has a free afternoon,” a PM told me in my first week.
challenge.body: Design was a small, stretched desk taking tickets from four product teams, with no shared library, no crit and no numbers leadership could read. Every PM had a direct line into a designer’s calendar, and work was judged by how fast it shipped. Leadership saw design as a cost line, so every headcount ask started from zero.

constraints: Four apps, four roadmaps, one design budget
Hybrid team: Vancouver office plus remote
No recruiter and no design-ops role

principles.title: Pods own outcomes; crit keeps us one team.
principles.body: Each pod answers for its app’s numbers. A weekly crit and one shared library stop four apps drifting into four products.

principles.title: Hire for judgement; train for tools.
principles.body: Scorecards before job posts, one written rubric for every panel, and a paid exercise that respects a candidate’s time.

principles.title: Leadership gets one page, every month.
principles.body: Shipped, moved, at risk, asks. If leadership has to ask what design did last month, the page has already failed.

decisions.why: Splitting designers by app made four silos and left no cover for a holiday. Pods group work by merchant problem: alerts and pre-orders, memberships and promotions, the AI assistant.
decisions.tradeoff: Designers trade some depth in a single app for breadth, and PMs share a pod’s time.
decisions.risk: Pod priorities clashing. Checked in the monthly capacity review; rebalanced twice in the year.

decisions.decision: A paid three-hour exercise instead of an unpaid take-home.
decisions.why: Unpaid take-homes took candidates eight to twelve hours and quietly filtered out parents and people with second jobs. A paid, timed exercise on a real problem showed judgement in three.
decisions.tradeoff: CA$300 per candidate and more of my calendar; fewer people reach the exercise stage.
decisions.risk: Inconsistent scoring. Every panellist scored the same written rubric, alone, before the debrief.
decisions.owner: Me, with people operations and a senior designer

decisions.why: Someone had to own the library, tooling and rituals, but a full-time ops role in a small team would have cost a designer seat on the product.
decisions.tradeoff: Ops became a rotating seat, one designer per quarter at 20% time, and the headcount went to a product designer.
decisions.risk: Library and tooling work slipping behind delivery. Watched through office-hours attendance and the definition of ready.

decisions.decision: A HEART scorecard per app, every month.
decisions.why: Leadership didn’t need to know how many screens we made. They needed to know whether merchants set up, came back and succeeded.
decisions.tradeoff: Slower to stand up: analytics events in four apps and a standing panel of 40 merchants. The first three briefs ran without merchant-panel numbers.
decisions.risk: Numbers nobody acts on. Any signal that changes no decision for two quarters is dropped.
decisions.owner: Me, with the PMs and our data analyst

process.heading: Three pods for four apps
body: My first month was a listening tour: every PM, every engineering lead and twenty merchant calls. Four apps were drifting into four products, and nobody could take a holiday.
I moved design to three pods and a shared research and content seat. Capacity is planned in designer-weeks every quarter and rebalanced with product when the bets change.

figure.caption: D1 · Q3 capacity by app: three pods across four apps, plus the research and content seat.

process.heading: One rubric, 38 days to offer
body: I wrote the role scorecards before the job posts, then ran every candidate through the same steps: a portfolio screen, a paid three-hour exercise and a panel scored on one written rubric.
240 people applied. Every offer we made was accepted, a median of 38 days from application to signed offer.

figure.caption: D2 · Same rubric, every panel: craft, product thinking and collaboration, scored before the debrief.

process.heading: Designer-weeks first, dollars second
body: I own the design budget: CA$180,000 a year outside salaries, for contractors, tools and licences, research incentives and learning. I plan capacity first, then dollars, and hold 8% in reserve for the quarter that goes sideways.
The hire I didn’t make was design ops. A rotating ops seat gave that headcount to a product designer.

figure.caption: D3 · No ops hire: a rotating ops seat, and an 8% reserve that covered a contractor when Promotions slipped.

process.heading: Numbers someone will act on
body: On the first working Monday of every month I gather a HEART scorecard for each app from product analytics, support tags and a standing panel of 40 merchants.
The team sees exactly what leadership sees. Every status is a word, so a red cell never needs a meeting to explain it.

figure.caption: D4 · September 2026: twenty signals, two at risk, each with a named owner.

process.heading: One page, every month
body: Leadership gets one page from me every month, two days after the scorecard: what shipped, what moved, what’s at risk and what I need. Twelve briefs in twelve months; the first three carried support and analytics numbers only, because the merchant panel took a quarter to stand up.
The asks on that page are how the design budget gets decided. When Promotions slipped, the risk, the fix and its cost were in the brief before anyone asked.

figure.caption: The September 2026 brief as it went to the leadership team.

process.heading: Rituals light enough to keep
body: A weekly crit, two design reviews with engineering, one shared library and a written definition of ready cut the time from design done to in development by 35%.
Every designer has a 1:1 every two weeks and a growth plan on a four-level ladder we wrote together. Designers now run crit without me.

figure.caption: Career ladder v1.2: one line per level and track, and a growth plan that ended in a promotion.

compare.caption: D1 · Same plan, same scale: one desk fielding four queues of tickets became three pods and a research seat around one library.

gallery.caption: D3 · The design budget month by month: under plan until the reserve paid for the Promotions contractor. Landed +2.4%.
D4 · Report gathering: every HEART signal has one source and one owner, checked before the brief goes up.
D1 · Q4 planning in designer-weeks: 71 asked, 62 available, and the 9 that moved to Q1 agreed with the PMs.
The team as a plan: three pods, a research seat and a library, joined by crit, review and 1:1 corridors.

after_launch.what: First hires in; crit every Tuesday
Shared library and a written definition of ready
No one has left, budget landed

not_taken: A designer per app. Simple to explain, but it made four silos and left no one to cover a holiday.
A design-team dashboard of screens shipped and tickets closed. It measured our activity, not the merchant’s outcome.
A full-time design-ops hire in a small team. A rotating seat did the job and kept a designer on the product.
reflections: I hired for judgement and it paid off, but I under-invested in onboarding. The first hires took eight weeks to ship on their own; a written 30-day plan got the next ones there in four.
Reporting up felt like overhead until the month it wasn’t. When Promotions slipped, the brief had already named the risk and the fix, and the budget conversation took ten minutes.

deeper.title: The hiring rubric
body: Each role had a one-page scorecard written before the post: three outcomes for the first year and the three competencies we would test — craft, product thinking and collaboration.
Panellists scored each competency from 1 to 4, alone and in writing, before the debrief. We hired at 3 or above on all three and 4 on at least one.

deeper.title: What goes in the monthly brief
body: Five headings on one page: Shipped, Moved, At risk, Asks, Next. Moved lists only numbers from the HEART scorecard. At risk always names a plan and an owner. Asks always carry a price or a person.
It goes out on the Wednesday after the scorecard lands, so the team and leadership argue from the same numbers.

deeper.title: How the ladder was written
body: Four levels by four tracks, one line each. I drafted it and the team rewrote it in two workshops; every designer placed themselves first, and we calibrate together each quarter.
Growth plans name one stretch responsibility per quarter, such as running crit or owning a pod’s onboarding.
